<reason>PRO (B) built a clean mechanism — frontier compute bottlenecks the training that fixes capability in next-generation military systems — and defended it through every round while turning CON's own language against it. CON's core route (military AI runs on mature nodes, so denial only buys commercial-lab friction) was plausible but never fully answered why a rational adversary would forgo frontier compute for military programs if available; PRO's "no separate military fab" and "a bet placed on the adversary's behalf" closed that gap. CON's "national emergency" phrasing became a liability that PRO's pressure questions exposed, and CON's "prestige industry" answer was a partial dodge. On cost, CON's "lost volume funds the next tool generation" was coherent but unshown against PRO's grounded record-order-book point, and CON effectively conceded the hole was unshown. Both sides misreferenced IDs in pressure questions (P2.x, C2.x), so no differential penalty. PRO made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A1 in Rebuttal 2 ("None—and that is the trick in the question. A fielded system is, by definition, already trained... the systems fielded in 2030 are being trained now") neutralized CON's strongest pressure question by reframing the motion around development rather than fielded inventory, then paired it with the budget-line/national-emergency contradiction that CON never cleanly escaped.</best_rebuttal>
